title: Python: Indentation defines code blocks
body: In Python, indentation defines code blocks. Code indented below statements like `if`, `for`, or `def` belongs to that structure. Since blocks aren’t enclosed in curly braces like in other languages, a single space of indentation can change the execution flow. Beginners often get confused about whether a `print` statement is inside or outside an `if` statement. When reading code, you must look at the leading spaces on each line to distinguish which code runs within a condition and which code always runs. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary guide to help you identify how variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, then categorize that line: is it a step that reads input, changes a value, evaluates a condition, or stores or outputs a result? Doing so allows you to apply the concepts learned from short examples to reading actual project code. Determine which lines fall under `if`, `for`, or `def` based on indentation depth. When reading code, check indentation boundaries before looking at parentheses. Even if lines appear to be on the same line, a single space difference can change the execution order, which is crucial for predicting output and analyzing errors.
when_to_show: if, for, def, Python Syntax Problems
detail: Indentation in Python is not merely a stylistic choice; it defines the boundaries of code blocks. Only lines indented to the same depth as the line following `if`, `for`, or `def` are included within that structure. When solving output prediction problems, first mark the indentation depth of each line, then distinguish between lines that execute only when the condition is true and those that always execute.

title: C: A language close to memory
body: C is often described as a language that is close to memory. While Python makes it relatively easy to work with lists and strings, C requires you to deal more directly with things like memory addresses, pointers, and array sizes. As a result, C allows you to create fast, low-level programs, but a single mistake can lead to memory errors. While Python learners don’t need to dive deep into C right away, understanding why terms like “stack,” “heap,” “byte,” and “pointer” are important can be helpful. This card is not intended merely for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you identify how these concepts relate to variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line of code where the concept appears, and then determine whether that line reads input, modifies a value, evaluates a condition, or stores or outputs a result. Doing so allows you to apply the concepts learned from short examples to reading actual project code. C is a language that operates close to memory, allowing for fast and precise control, but mistakes can be critical. When reading code, you must verify that aspects such as pointers, array bounds, and memory deallocation are handled safely.
detail: C is a language that deals with memory addresses, array sizes, and pointers in a relatively direct way. While this allows you to create fast, low-level programs, out-of-bounds access and memory deallocation errors can be dangerous. When studying Python, it’s helpful to understand terms like “byte,” “stack,” “heap,” and “pointer” by relating them to the C-style memory model.

title: Java: Class-Based Structure
body: Java is a language that makes extensive use of a class-based structure. A class can be thought of as a blueprint that bundles data and functionality together. Although Python also has classes, beginners often learn functions, dictionaries, and lists first before moving on to classes. When reviewing Java code, you should pay attention to file and class names, methods, and the object creation flow. This concept later ties into understanding object-oriented programming. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you identify how these concepts—such as variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows—are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, and then determine whether that line reads input, modifies a value, evaluates a condition, or stores or outputs a result. Doing so allows you to apply the concepts learned from short examples to reading actual project code. Java is a language that organizes code around classes. It groups data and behavior together within a class and creates objects to handle actual values. While Python also supports classes, this structure appears more frequently as a fundamental pattern in Java. When reading code, you must distinguish between which classes represent the design and which objects represent the actual values.
when_to_show: Class, Object-Oriented Programming, Type Comparison Problems
detail: Java has a strong class-centric approach to organizing files and code. A class is a blueprint that bundles data and behavior, while an object is the actual instance created from that blueprint. When reading code, you can grasp its structure by checking, in order, the file name, class name, method name, constructor calls, and which variables the objects are assigned to.

title: JavaScript: The Web Browser's Default Language
body: JavaScript is the primary language of web browsers. While HTML defines the structure of the page and CSS determines its appearance, JavaScript handles actions such as button clicks, page transitions, data loading, and saving to localStorage. If a Python learning app runs as a PWA, JavaScript in the browser can read the lesson JSON and display the cards. When reading the code, it’s easier to understand JavaScript by focusing on the parts that connect user actions to screen changes. These cards aren’t just for memorizing word definitions; they serve as supplementary explanations to help you see how these concepts relate to variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code. Doing so allows you to apply the concepts learned from short examples to reading actual project code. JavaScript is the core language that handles screen interactions and data requests in the browser. When reading code, examining event listeners, DOM manipulation, `fetch` requests, and the order of asynchronous processing reveals the flow of a web application.
detail: JavaScript is a language that connects the user interface and user actions in a browser. It handles visible actions and data flow, such as button clicks, DOM changes, `fetch` requests, and `localStorage` storage. When reading web app code, you should check where events are registered, which functions are executed, and when asynchronous results are reflected on the screen.

title: SQL: Structured Query Language
body: SQL is a query language used to send queries to tabular databases. SELECT retrieves data, WHERE sets conditions, ORDER BY sorts the data, and LIMIT restricts the number of rows returned. For example, you can use SQL to find a specific student’s problem-solving history or a list of problems of a certain difficulty level. In Python code, you can either construct SQL strings or execute them indirectly through an ORM. When reading code, you should verify which table the data is retrieved from and under what conditions. This card is not intended merely for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how these concepts relate to variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, and then determine whether that line reads input, modifies values, evaluates conditions, or stores or outputs results. Doing so allows you to apply the concepts learned from short examples to reading actual project code. SQL is a query language used to find specific rows and columns in tabular data. When reading code, you should check what is being retrieved with `SELECT`, what is being filtered with `WHERE`, and which tables are being joined with `JOIN`.
detail: SQL is a query language used to find specific rows and columns in tabular data. "SELECT" refers to the values to be retrieved, "FROM" refers to the target table, "WHERE" refers to the conditions, and "JOIN" refers to joining tables. When reading code, it is important to look beyond the SQL string itself and verify which user inputs are included in the conditions and how the results are transformed into a data structure.

title: Cypher: Neo4j Graph Database Query Language
body: Cypher is a query language used to find nodes and relationships in the Neo4j graph database. While SQL is widely used to retrieve rows from tabular data, Cypher focuses on exploring which nodes are connected by which relationships within a graph. For example, you can find which concept nodes a student node is connected to, or identify the “athlete” concept associated with a specific concept. When reading code, Cypher often uses parentheses to represent nodes and arrows to indicate the direction of relationships. This card is not intended merely for memorizing definitions; rather, it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how these elements—such as variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows—interact within actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, and then determine whether that line reads input, modifies values, evaluates conditions, or stores or outputs results. Doing so allows you to apply the concepts learned from short examples to reading actual project code. Cypher is a query language used in graph databases to find nodes and relationships as patterns. When reading the code, just remember that parentheses represent nodes and arrows represent relationships. The direction of the relationship is also important.
detail: Cypher is a query language used to find nodes and relationship patterns in graph databases such as Neo4j. Parentheses often denote nodes, while square brackets or arrows typically represent relationships and their directions. When reading the code, you must identify the starting node, determine how many steps to follow along a relationship, and distinguish whether the returned value is a node or a path.

title: Rust: Striving for Both Safety and Performance
body: Rust is a language that aims to combine safety and performance. While it allows you to write fast programs like C or C++, it also enforces strict rules to minimize memory-related errors. As a result, it has garnered attention in the fields of system programming, servers, blockchain, and embedded systems. Python learners don’t need to learn Rust right away, but it helps to understand why Rust is mentioned when you come across terms like data types, ownership, and memory safety. This card is not intended merely for memorizing definitions; rather, it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you see how these concepts—such as variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows—are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where the concept appears, then categorize that line: is it a step that reads input, modifies a value, evaluates a condition, or stores or outputs a result? Doing so allows you to apply the concepts learned from short examples to reading actual project code. In particular, ownership and borrowing rules are rigorously checked to minimize errors in code that directly handles memory. Although the syntax is stricter than Python’s, this approach has the advantage of catching many errors before execution. When reading code, it is important to consider where ownership of values lies.
detail: Rust is a language designed to enforce strict memory safety while maintaining performance. Although its ownership and borrowing rules may seem strict at first, they have the advantage of catching many errors before execution. When reading code, it is important to consider who owns a value, how long a reference remains in memory, and whether it is a mutable reference.

title: Go: A language well-suited for servers and cloud tools

There are also many tools built with Go in cloud ecosystems such as Docker and Kubernetes. As a Python learner, you don’t need to have an in-depth understanding of Go code right away, but it’s good to keep in mind that you’ll likely come across the name “Go” frequently when reading documentation on server tools or infrastructure. title: PowerShell: Windows Automation Shell
body: PowerShell is a widely used automation shell on Windows. It allows you to perform tasks such as navigating folders, deleting files, running scripts, executing Git commands, and running Python code using commands. PowerShell often uses backticks for line continuation, and the default path notation follows the Windows convention. In development work, even for the same Python code, the command syntax may differ depending on whether it is executed in PowerShell or Bash. Therefore, you should check your current shell before pasting commands. title: Bash: The default shell for Linux/Ubuntu
body: Bash is the default shell commonly used in Linux and Ubuntu environments. Like PowerShell, you can use commands to navigate folders, view files, and run programs. When running Python projects on a server, you’ll frequently encounter Bash commands. For example, you’ll use commands like `cd`, `ls`, `cat`, `grep`, and `python`. When reading code, a Bash script isn’t Python code itself, but it can serve as an operational procedure that specifies the order in which Python is executed. When reading code, you should check for path separators, environment variable notation, pipes, and redirection. It may not be directly compatible with PowerShell commands.
detail: Bash is a shell commonly used on Linux and Ubuntu servers. In addition to commands such as `cd`, `ls`, `cat`, `grep`, and `python`, pipes, redirection, and environment variable notation frequently appear. Although Bash scripts are not Python code per se, they demonstrate the sequence in which the environment is set up and executed, so they should be read as operational procedures.

title: A function is a small task box
summary: You can think of a function as a small box of code that takes an input, performs a specific task, and returns a result.
detail: A function is a small "task box" that takes input, performs a specific operation, and returns a result. "def" is the keyword used to define a function, and the values inside the parentheses are passed in as parameters or arguments. "return" sends the result of the calculation back to the outside. When reading long code, identifying the function name, input values, internal processing, and return value first helps you see the flow.
examples: def add(a, b): return a + b
Input: a, b / Output: return value
body: It’s easier to understand functions if you think of them as small task boxes. When you feed a value into one, it processes it in a specific order and then returns the result or displays it on the screen. For example, `len('Python')` is a function that returns 6 when a string is passed to it. When reading a function, you shouldn’t just look at the function name; you need to distinguish what input goes inside the parentheses, whether the function returns a value, or if it displays the result on the screen like `print` does. Beginners often get confused between a function’s return value and screen output. `result = len(items)` stores the length in a variable, whereas `print(result)` displays that value on the screen. Understanding this difference will help you reliably interpret the input, processing, and output structure when you create your own functions later on.
